summary: Teaches children to find the area of compound rectilinear shapes (L- and T-shapes) by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles, finding each rectangle's area by multiplying, and summing. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing internal side from the given outer measurements. This rests on two prior ideas: area is additive, and rectangle area is found by multiplying rows by columns. For the worked example, a 3 m × 5 m rectangle gives 15 m² and a 2 m × 4 m rectangle gives 8 m², summing to 23 m². The sub-areas are ADDED (not multiplied) because area is additive.
misconceptions: Treats the figure as one big rectangle — multiplies the outer bounding dimensions as if the notch weren't there
Overlaps the two sub-rectangles and double-counts the shared corner
Cannot find a sub-rectangle's side when it isn't printed
Adds side lengths / a perimeter-like total instead of areas, or drops the square unit

activities.title: Cut the L-shaped floor plan into rectangles
steps: Look at an L-shaped room on a grid with its outer measurements labelled.
Draw a cut line to split the shape into two non-overlapping rectangles.
Find each sub-rectangle's area by multiplying its sides (e.g. 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m²).
Add the two areas to get the total, keeping square-metre units (23 m²).
Say why the two areas are ADDED rather than multiplied: each rectangle covers a separate part of the floor, and area is additive.
Re-cut the same shape a different valid way and confirm the total is still 23 m².
activities.insight: A rectilinear figure can be split into non-overlapping rectangles whose areas ADD to the whole; the pieces are summed (not multiplied) because area is additive, and any valid split gives the same total.

activities.title: Find the hidden internal side
steps: Look at a compound shape (which may be a separate illustrative figure, not the earlier floor plan) where one internal side is left blank and only the outer measurements are printed.

Work out which outer measurements determine the missing internal length by subtracting; for example, 5 − 3 = 2 is a generic illustration of taking one printed outer length from another, not the derivation of a hidden side in the 23 m² floor plan (whose hidden sides come from 5 − 2 = 3 and 7 − 3 = 4).
Mark the derived length on the figure.
Complete the decomposition and compute the total area.
activities.insight: A sub-rectangle's unlabelled side can be derived by reasoning about the outer lengths, not guessed or taken only from printed numbers.

activities.title: Spot the whole-rectangle error
steps: Examine a worked solution where someone multiplied the outer bounding dimensions (e.g. 5×7 = 35 m²) as if the notch weren't there, or multiplied every printed number together.
Explain what that person forgot about the shape.
Overlay or imagine a grid and count: the tiles in the missing corner are not there.
Give the correct total by decomposing first (15 + 8 = 23 m²).
activities.insight: Multiplying the outer bounding dimensions — or multiplying all the printed numbers together — counts tiles the shape does not contain; the missing notch must be accounted for, and here we do that by decomposing the shape into rectangles before multiplying each piece.

activities.title: Covering versus going around
steps: Tile one sub-rectangle and count the square units inside it.
Contrast that with tracing around the edges of the whole figure.
State whether the task asks for area (tiles inside) or perimeter (distance around), and answer with the correct square units.
activities.insight: Area counts the squares covering the inside and is reported in square units; adding up the edges gives a perimeter-like total, which is a different quantity.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch how the child decomposes. Present an L-shaped room drawn on paper with the outer measurements labelled — overall it is a 3 m × 5 m rectangle with a 2 m × 4 m rectangle joined on, and one internal length is left blank so it must be worked out. Say: 'Find the total area of this room. Show me how you split it up.' Watch them partition, find each area, sum, and handle the missing side; then ask them to split it a different way.
checkAnswer: Draws a decomposition into two non-overlapping rectangles, derives the unlabelled internal length from the given outer lengths, computes 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m², sums to 23 m² keeping square-metre units, and can show that a different valid split gives the same 23 m².
